10148-the-merry-adventures-of-robin-hood:
Howard Pyle's Merry Adventures of Robin Hood opens with an address to the reader, warning serious folk who think life has nothing to do with innocent laughter to close the book. Those who go on will meet good, sober folk of real history frisking in gay colors, including a stout, lusty Henry II and a fair, gentle lady.

Set in merry England in the time of old King Henry the Second, the tales follow Robin from the greenwood dawn of Maytime through outlawry, friendship, and archery. Pyle's pictures and prose made this the classic Robin Hood. Readers of all ages get the outlaw at his merriest and most generous.
10321-dragon-s-blood:
Henry Milner Rideout published this romance in 1909, with pictures by Harold M. Brett. Its opening letter nods to Kipling's tale of Kafiristan, then promises a slighter, stranger bag of tricks. The story moves between town life, pagodas, and war boards, with a lady, a griffin, and a pied piper among its early signs.

Sword play, a hot night, a siege, and a figure called Kau Fai carry the plot through peril and intrigue. Love, loyalty, and honor thread the action, in the manner of early twentieth-century adventure fiction. Readers get a colorful, fast-moving romance of the exotic East, told with verve.
10463-the-little-house-in-the-fairy-wood:
Ethel Cook Eliot wrote this children's fantasy for Torka and Northwind, opening on a cold morning when Eric is shaken awake by Mrs. Freg at six o'clock. Eric shares a bed with two other boys, and his day begins like any other, yet it will become the beginning of all things new. The fairy wood waits beyond the house.

Magic in a mist, a bright house, firelight, gossip, world stories, and a witch at the window fill later chapters. Tree mothers, wind hunts, and spring wanderings carry Eric deeper into wonder. Readers get a gentle, lyrical fantasy of childhood, nature, and magic.
10846-seekers-after-god:
F. W. Farrar, canon of Westminster, wrote Seekers After God about pagan thinkers who reached toward truths Christianity would later proclaim. The book opens with Seneca of Cordova, on the Baetis under the Sierra Morena, in a city Augustus honored as the Patrician Colony. Spain gave Rome emperors Trajan, Hadrian, and Theodosius, and writers from Columella to Quintilian.

Farrar sets Seneca among Stoics who sought a higher life through reason, duty, and self-command. His tone is reverent and scholarly, quoting a French critic on Seneca's cloud fringed with rays. Readers get a humane study of philosophy on the edge of faith.
10889-the-life-and-romances-of-mrs-eliza:
George Frisbie Whicher wrote this 1915 study of Eliza Haywood, a prolific London novelist of the early 1700s. Haywood left almost no record of her own life, so Whicher builds her story from scant facts, her books, and contemporary gossip. Chapters trace her from short romances of passion through scandal novels and secret histories to later domestic fiction.

Along the way, Whicher explains her part in the Duncan Campbell pamphlets, her attack by Pope in The Dunciad, and her essays and letters. He also judges which works matter and why her reputation faded. The monograph suits readers of early English fiction, offering both a life pieced together from fragments and a clear guide to a very large body of work.
11044-the-existence-of-god:
Francois de Salignac de la Mothe-Fenelon, Archbishop of Cambrai, argued for God's existence in this classic work, here in an English translation transcribed by David Price. Fenelon admits that metaphysical proofs, tracing things to first principles, suit few minds, since their very simplicity escapes those unused to pure thought. Moral proofs, drawn from nature, suit everyone.

Opening the eyes, Fenelon says, shows art throughout nature, and wisdom stamped on all creatures points to a maker, just as the soul's power over the body points beyond itself. St. Augustine's reflections on the body and soul support the case. The book offers a gentle, popular philosophy of religion, aimed at readers who reason from what they see rather than from abstract ideas.
11097-young-robin-hood:
G. Manville Fenn wrote this boys' adventure about Robin Hood as a boy, with twenty-three illustrations. Young Robin rides behind a sour serving man named David, wriggling on a slippery horse through a dark forest of oak and beech. David warns of robbers, and Robin answers that he would like to meet Robin Hood himself.

Forest pools, golden carp, pike, and dragonflies fill the journey, and Robin's boldness marks him out early. Fenn imagines the outlaw's childhood as a tale of courage, humour, and woodland adventure, suitable for young readers. The book gives the Robin Hood legend a fresh start, with a boy hero learning the forest before he leads its men.
11268-the-flood:
Part of the Old Testament Scenes and Narratives series, a second series of the Good Child's Library, this 1851 Philadelphia children's book retells the Flood in fifteen short chapters. Contents move from the wickedness of man and Noah's command to build the ark. through the opening windows of heaven and the floating ark, to the raven and dove, Noah's sacrifice, and the bow in the clouds. Illustrations in oil colors accompanied the text.

Hogan, Perkins and Company planned the series to match their New Testament volumes, offering children a scriptural library in uniform style. The Flood's language is simple and its episodes brief, suited to reading aloud. For historians of children's publishing, it shows Bible stories packaged as attractive, illustrated gift books.
12038-representative-plays-by-american-d:
Montrose J. Moses's Representative Plays by American Dramatists, 1856 to 1911, edited with an introduction to each play, appeared in 1921 with portraits and original playbills. Moses dedicates the volume to Brander Matthews, friend of the American theatre, to whom all critics of the theatre are beholden.

The table of contents opens with an introduction and bibliographies, then Rip Van Winkle, a legend of the Catskills, in a comparative arrangement with the Kerr version. Moses's anthology argues, by selection, that American drama had a history worth studying, from melodrama and comedy to the more serious plays of the early twentieth century.
12475-fires-of-driftwood:
Isabel Ecclestone MacKay's verse collection, first published in Toronto in 1922, gathers poems that had appeared in magazines from Harper's and Scribner's to Canadian journals. Decorations by J. E. H. MacDonald frame lyrics with titles such as Fires of Driftwood, When as a Lad, A Pilgrim and The Homesteader.

Nature, seasons and travel supply much of the imagery, from spring and autumn gardens to wet weather and a crocus bed. Other poems turn to loss, fear, resurrection and a lost name, keeping a reflective, often Canadian, note. The volume reads as a working poet's harvest, magazine pieces brought together into one book of short, musical lyrics.
13526-in-the-clutch-of-the-war-god:
Milo Hastings imagines a future war in this tale from Physical Culture magazine, July to September 1911, framed as the Humaniculture Society's history of the twentieth century. The Orient invades the Occident, and America, self-satisfied and deaf to lessons of Oriental progress, faces the cost of complacency.

Ethel watches a great squadron move eastward, with men and women trained as aviators and a fan-ventilated gymnasium as the ship's most conspicuous fitting. Cities drop conflagration bombs on shingled roofs and prussic acid into reservoirs, while an American army gathers in a giant semicircle from coast to coast. Hastings writes invasion fiction as warning, not celebration.
13775-every-step-in-canning-the-cold-pac:
Grace Viall Gray, a former home economics teacher at Iowa State College, wrote this 1920 manual on canning. It teaches the cold-pack method step by step, from getting ready to storing finished jars. Chapters cover soft fruits, hard fruits, vegetables, soups, jellies, meat, and fish. Later sections add drying, brining, curing, and home storage.

Gray stresses clean jars, correct heat, and safe seals. She explains why canned goods spoil and how to prevent it. Tips on racks, jar holders, and marketing home-canned food help beginners and sellers alike. The book reflects wartime thrift and the rise of home science teaching. It remains a clear, practical guide to preserving food at home.
13916-marie-bashkirtseff-from-childhood-:
Mary J. Safford translated this selection from Marie Bashkirtseff's journals, covering childhood to girlhood. Bashkirtseff began writing at twelve, ingenuously and sincerely, amusing readers with whims and touching them with sufferings. Notebooks bound in white parchment, slightly discoloured, held her early writing. Editors chose first books for their revelation of a young girl's mind.

Marie prays for blessings and for love, imagining a beloved dead with tears in her eyes. Her enthusiasms, vanities, and sorrows fill the pages. The journal later made her famous as an artist and diarist who died young. This volume suits readers of diaries and women's lives. It shows a gifted girl thinking aloud.
13982-cap-n-abe-storekeeper-a-story-of-c:
James A. Cooper wrote Cap'n Abe, Storekeeper in 1917, a Cape Cod story of shop, sea, and romance. Cap'n Abe runs his store and living room, where neighbours gather. Chapters follow a choice, a shadow of coming events, and what happened in the night. Boarded by pirates, suspicion, and salt water taffy add humour.

Louise Grayling, hobbled by city life for nearly a year, craves new scenes and gives up a furnished apartment. Aunt Euphemia descends, Washy Gallup grows curious, and discoveries follow. Cooper writes Cape Cod speech and custom with affection. The novel suits readers of regional romance. Its storekeeper hero anchors a warm community tale.
14026-spiritual-life-and-the-word-of-god:
Emanuel Swedenborg's Spiritual Life and the Word of God, extracted from Apocalypse Explained, sets out his theology in three parts. Part one treats spiritual life: how it is acquired, goods of charity, shunning evils, and cleansing the inside. Part two expounds the commandments one by one. Part three treats profanations of good and truth.

Swedenborg argues that church building and hospitals count as good only when done without hope of reward. Works done by man alone, or for reward, fail his test. The book presents Swedenborgian doctrine in systematic form. It suits readers of mysticism and Christian thought. The extracts offer a clear entry to a difficult author.
14076-the-elephant-god:
A rogue elephant in the Terai forest sets Gordon Casserly's 1921 adventure in motion, starting from a secret mission. Dedicated to a real killer elephant, the book follows Major Dermot through rajahs' palaces, Bhuttia raids, and the rescue of Noreen. A girl of the Terai, a rajah who covets an Englishwoman, and a feast of the goddess Kali raise the stakes chapter by chapter.

Love tangles with empire politics. The Rajah of Lalpuri, thwarted by his Dewan, demands the girl he saw at a durbar in Jalpaiguri and hires clever men to find a way. Dermot dances, sups, and hides in cardrooms while danger gathers. Casserly knew the frontier world he staged, and the novel moves at adventure pace: elephants, temples, palaces of death, and a tempest. Romance and peril share the work evenly throughout.
14563-sheila-of-big-wreck-cove-a-story-o:
James A. Cooper's 1922 Cape Cod story centers on Sheila of Big Wreck Cove, a girl caught in the life of a fishing village of captains, Portuguese workers, and summer visitors. The book first ran as a serial in 1921.

Cap'n Ira and Prue open the tale, and chapters follow the captain of the Seamew and the Latham house. A harvest home festival brings Tunis, a friendly local who helps a newcomer's niece settle with the Balls. Cooper writes with affection for Cape speech and shore life. The novel is a warm regional romance, salted with wreck lore and village gossip.
14566-elsie-s-motherhood:
Martha Finley's Elsie's Motherhood, the fifth Elsie volume, published in 1876, continues Elsie's life into motherhood in the South of 1867 and 1868. The preface notes that Ku Klux doings were added for a truer picture of those years.

Elsie guides her children Vi and others with prayer, tears, and gentle correction, urging kind thoughts toward cousins and gifts from pocket money. The household scenes are warm and pious, in Finley's familiar manner. The book pleased the series' many admirers, and it shows Reconstruction-era domestic fiction from a conservative Southern viewpoint. Finley's readers followed Elsie from girlhood to motherhood.
14573-the-truce-of-god:
Mary Roberts Rinehart's short 1920 tale is set in a medieval town at Christmas, where the Church's Truce of God forbids fighting from Thursday evening to Monday morning. The town celebrates with a roast steer, fruit, and vegetables.

A young overlord sulks in his cliff-top castle, nursing a grievance, while a bishop seeks to soften him and teach what matters beyond war and pride. Rinehart writes the legend in simple, tender prose, with illustrations by Harold Sichel. The story preaches peace at the year's darkest festival, and it remains a gentle holiday fable.
14874-elsie-s-womanhood:
Martha Finley's Elsie's Womanhood, a sequel to Elsie's Girlhood, was called for so loudly that the author undertook it with pleasure. Dates compelled bringing in the late war, the American Civil War, and Finley strives to wound no feelings, to stay as impartial as if writing history.

Her aim is a true, though faint, picture of great losses and sufferings on both sides. She hopes the thought of renewing the awful strife will become utterly abhorrent to every lover of peace. Elsie, now a woman, faces war, family and faith with the moral steadiness readers knew from her girlhood. The complete authorised edition keeps that earnest, domestic tone intact.
14946-the-blossoming-rod:
Mary Stewart Cutting's short Christmas story follows Mr. Langshaw, who senses unusual preparations for a gift to him this year. Children keep asking him for change to pay for services rendered, and dollars and cents enter the family's Christmas festivities as they enter daily life.

Langshaw stops as usual to look at a sporting goods display on his way home, on the Friday before Christmas Monday. He touches a ten-dollar bill in his pocket and wonders what the gift will be. A rod flapped in circles in the backyard, shown in an illustration, hints at the answer. Cutting writes a gentle tale of family calculation, affection and a present that blossoms beyond its price.
14961-sentimental-tommy-the-story-of-his:
J. M. Barrie's 1896 story of Tommy's boyhood opens with Tommy contriving to keep one out, first seen on a dirty London stair at five, in sexless garments that were all he had. He must be looked at sideways, lest he sit down hurriedly to hide them.

That inscrutable face, which later made clubmen uneasy and puzzled ladies while he made love to them, is already his, except when he smiles at a pretty face. Barrie, author of The Little Minister and A Window in Thrums, follows Tommy from London to Thrums and through a boyhood of sentiment, mischief and imagination. The novel is a portrait of a future writer in the making.
15583-adventures-of-buffalo-bill-from-bo:
Colonel Prentiss Ingraham wrote this dime novel of Buffalo Bill. Beadle and Adams of New York published it weekly in 1881. It was number one of Beadle's Boy's Library of Sport, Story and Adventure. It cost five cents, at two dollars fifty a year, and promised truth stranger than fiction. The subtitle calls Cody the monarch of bordermen.

Deeds of daring, scenes of thrilling peril, and romantic incidents trace Cody's early life from boyhood to manhood. An illustration shows a maddened bull bounding into the air, goring those in advance, and leading the herd. The prologue opens by insisting truth beats fiction. The book is classic dime-novel biography: a frontier hero built for boys, in fast, breathless episodes of danger and pluck.
15622-handbook-on-japanning-2nd-edition-:
William N. Brown wrote this handbook on japanning for ironware, tinware, wood, and more, with sections on tin-plating and galvanizing. Scott, Greenwood and Son of London published the second edition, revised and enlarged with thirteen illustrations, in January 1913, with D. Van Nostrand in New York. The first edition, under the title A Handbook on Japanning and Enamelling, appeared in 1901.

Four sections cover the craft in order. The introduction teaches priming and preparing surfaces, and a first stage for wood or leather without priming. Japan grounds follow in white, blue, scarlet, red, yellow, green, orange, purple, and black, with tortoise-shell ground, painting, and varnishing. Japanning metals, enamelling bedstead frames, and japanning tin trays close the early sections. The book is a practical trade manual for a decorative craft now largely lost.
1564-boswell-s-life-of-johnson-abridged-:
James Boswell's Life of Johnson, here abridged and edited by Charles Grosvenor Osgood of Princeton, follows Samuel Johnson through London coffee houses, Grub Street hack work. The making of his great Dictionary. Boswell, Johnson's young Scottish friend, records his talk, his quarrels, and his kindnesses with unmatched fidelity.

Osgood's abridgement cuts most legal opinions, many letters, and Boswell's own notes, keeping the conversations and scenes that show Johnson alive. The result is a shorter road into a very long classic. It remains the best first version of the most famous biography in English.
15652-the-poetical-works-of-thomas-hood:
William Michael Rossetti edited this enlarged and revised edition of the poetical works of Thomas Hood, published in New York by A. L. Burt Company. Rossetti's biographical introduction opens by noting how few outward events marked Hood's life: life-long ill health, and one commercial failure with consequent expatriation. Beyond that, little presents itself for record in an upright, beneficial career, bright with genius and wit, dark with death's lengthening shadow.

Contents run from To Hope, The Departure of Summer, and The Sea of Death through Lycus the Centaur, Fair Ines, and sonnets on silence and death. I Remember, I Remember, The Plea of the Midsummer Fairies, and Hero and Leander follow. Hood's father, a London publisher and bookseller, reprinted old works and published Bloomfield. The volume gathers a beloved Victorian poet's lyrics, ballads, and comic verse in one place.
15933-stories-of-childhood:
A children's anthology in the Little Classics series, edited by Rossiter Johnson, issued by Houghton Mifflin in Boston and New York in 1914. Copyright dates to 1875, with James R. Osgood and Company. Johnson gathers tales of childhood by famous hands, each short enough for reading aloud. The Riverside Press printed the volume.

A Dog of Flanders by Ouida leads, with Ruskin's King of the Golden River and Elizabeth Stuart Phelps's Lady of Shalott. Marjorie Fleming by John Brown, Little Jakey, and Henry Kingsley's Lost Child follow, with John Neal, Rebecca Harding Davis, and Dickens's Child's Dream of a Star. The book gives a Victorian shelf of childhood: tender, moral, and made to be remembered.
16180-roman-mosaics-or-studies-in-rome-a:
Hugh Macmillan's Roman Mosaics, published by Macmillan in London and New York in 1888, studies Rome and its neighborhood in linked essays. Chapter one walks to church in Rome. It passes a country walk and a town residence, the Piazza di Spagna, the staircase, and beggars. Flowers, the Via Babuino, and the Pincian Hill lead on to the Villa Borghese and Ponte Molle. Chapter two takes the Appian Way, its tombs, its lonely country, and its gates.

Macmillan, author of Bible Teachings in Nature, joins travel, history, and devotion in a minister's observant voice. Each mosaic piece sets a Roman scene beside a reflection. Readers planning an armchair visit to Rome will find a warm, learned companion.
16478-records-of-a-girlhood:
Frances Ann Kemble, the famed actress, draws on thousands of her own letters, written over forty years, for this 1880 memoir. Portions first ran in the Atlantic Monthly, with much new matter added and the whole revised. The girlhood chapters recall her youth, her stage life, and the people who shaped her.

Kemble writes with frankness and wit, and the letters give the book a direct, personal voice. Theater history, family life, and social scenes of the early nineteenth century all pass through her pages. Readers who like memoirs built from real letters will find this one vivid and unguarded.
16585-charred-wood:
Myles Muredach's 1917 novel opens with the Lady of the Tree and a monsignore, then winds through suspicion, Killimaga, bitter bread, and a bishop's confession. Who is Ruth, and why does a duchess abdicate, are the puzzles at the center, with an abduction, thin ice, and a beckoning hand along the way. The title asks whether God must char wood before He can draw with it.

The tale mixes Catholic atmosphere with mystery and romance, in the popular style of its day. The pace is brisk, the scenes shift from cliffs to confessionals, and the close ties the threads. Readers of old-fashioned mystery romance will find it colorful and absorbing.
16591-unity-of-good:
Mary Baker Eddy, author of Science and Health, sets out Christian Science teaching in this volume, copyrighted 1887, 1891, and 1908. Contents ask whether God knows sin, sickness, and death, whether anything real meets the physical senses, and whether there is death. A credo closes the questions: belief in God, man, matter, woman, and evil, with a summary of unity of good.

Eddy writes as a religious founder stating doctrine plainly for followers. The book is short and systematic, meant for study rather than casual reading. Readers of American religion will find a core text of Christian Science in its author's own words.
17434-the-thin-red-line-and-blue-blood:
Arthur Griffiths, author of chronicles of Newgate prison, issued this two-volume novel in London in 1886. The first volume opens in Paris, where a commissary is called, an arrest follows, and talk of war grows until soldiers head off to fight. Battles, a costly victory, a November gale, and the Golden Horn carry the action through courts, camps, and high society.

The second volume turns to secret service work, Cossacks, a fortress, Paris, Lincoln's Inn, and married life, closing with a short piece called Blue Blood. Readers get a broad Victorian war and intrigue novel, mixing battle scenes with spying, family ties, and social rank. Its sweep across two volumes gives the period a full stage.
18896-faith-gartney-s-girlhood:
Mrs. A. D. T. Whitney wrote this novel of a girl's growing up, issued in New York in 1913 by the New York Book Company. Whitney was known for The Gayworthys and A Summer in Leslie Goldthwaite's Life. The chapters trace Faith Gartney from money worries and sortes through aunts, neighbors, and new duties, toward a niche in life and a woman to fill it.

Along the way come a drive with the doctor, frost wonders, snow, a game at chess, and questions answered in conflict. Whitney's heroine learns through work, care for others, and patient endurance. Readers get a wholesome, old-fashioned novel of girlhood, written for young women, with a warm view of family, friendship, and moral growth.
19418-confessions-of-boyhood:
John Albee wrote this memoir of a New England boyhood, published in the early nineteen hundreds. Short chapters recall a small house, school days, church funerals, woods and pastures, and the long shadow of the Dorr War and the Millerite stir. His mother, his uncle, and the working men around him all stand out in clear portraits.

Later chapters follow the boy into trades: the sawmill, bootmaking, shop work, teaching, and farm labor. The book is less a life story in full than a set of scenes from youth, kept for what they show of work, faith, and home in rural America.
1965-captain-blood:
Rafael Sabatini's Captain Blood follows Peter Blood, an Irish doctor sold into slavery in Barbados after the Monmouth Rebellion. He escapes with fellow slaves to become the most feared pirate of the Caribbean. Blood's honor, his surgery, and his sword carry him through battles, betrayals, and a love affair with the governor's niece.

Sabatini writes the pirate romance with dash and with care for ships, law, and medicine. Blood himself — a gentleman forced into piracy — gives the book its moral center. The novel made Sabatini famous, and it remains the model for every pirate hero who is really a gentleman in disguise.
19805-the-tale-of-mr-tod:
Beatrix Potter published The Tale of Mr. Tod in 1912. Mr. Tod is a fox, and Tommy Brock is a badger. Brock only occasionally eats rabbit pie, the tale confides. He takes very little young ones when other food is really scarce. Brock and old Mr. Bouncer share a dislike of the wicked otters and Mr. Tod. They often talk over that painful subject together.

Mr. Tod is among Potter's darkest tales. Benjamin Bunny's children are stolen for a fox's supper. Tommy Brock, no hero himself, becomes the rescue. Potter wrote it for older children and kept the danger real. Her watercolors and prose stay exact and unsentimental. It is a summit of her art.
20157-the-call-of-the-blood:
Robert Hichens published The Call of the Blood in 1905, a novel of love and fate. A woman takes letters from her writing-table drawer with care. She awaits a visit from their writer, Emile Artois, that day. He has wired that he comes from Paris by night train and boat.

Hichens sets much of the tale in Sicily, under a hot southern sun. The call of the blood means deep pulls of race, place, and passion. His characters feel forces they can barely name or resist. Readers get lush, tense romance in the style that made Hichens famous.
20219-the-lion-s-brood:
Duffield Osborne published The Lion's Brood in 1901, a novel of ancient Rome. A man wakes to find a coin turned in his hand as he dozed. Its reverse shows a horseman in full armor at the gallop. The rider brandishes a naked sword and grips a severed head by its hair.

That grim coin sets the tone for a tale of Rome's hard men. Osborne wrote of eagles, legions, and the brood that Rome bred for war. Battles and honor codes drive his Romans far more than ease. Readers get a vivid, blood-stained romance of the ancient world.
20846-handwork-in-wood:
Thanks to tool firms in New Haven, Chicago, and Beloit open William Noyes's Handwork in Wood. Their loan of electrotypes helped the book's many plates take shape. Stanley Rule and Level of New Britain stands among those thanked by name.

Noyes, a teacher at Teachers College, wrote a full guide to wood craft. Timber, tools, joints, and design unfold in set order with clear plates. The book served school shops that taught hand skill as mind training. Its mix of craft lore and teaching method still speaks to woodworkers who learn best by doing, step by careful step.
21074-afloat-on-the-flood:
Lawrence J. Leslie set this boys' novel in the town of Carson, where spring rain has sent the Evergreen River on the rampage. Published in Chicago in 1915, it follows young Max and his friends as floodwater rises around their homes. Chapters move from weather reports at the post office to rescues on a shaking bridge.

The boys lend a helping hand, shelter in a half-drowned farmhouse, and take refuge on a roof. Later they defend their camp against a wild dog pack and face unwelcome guests. The flood itself is the main villain, and the story ends as the waters fall.
2142-childhood:
Leo Tolstoy begins his semi-autobiographical trilogy with Childhood, translated by C. J. Hogarth, opening on a boy's tenth birthday in August. His tutor Karl Ivanitch wakes him by slapping the wall with a fly-flap, knocking a dead fly onto his curls. Tolstoy wrote Childhood in the 1850s, drawing on his own boyhood at Yasnaya Polyana.

From that small scene Tolstoy builds a whole world of family, servants, lessons, and first feelings, told with exact memory. The book charms by its honesty about a child's mind, and it points toward the great novels that followed. The tutor Karl Ivanitch, kind and foolish by turns, stands for the child's first view of adults.
21697-the-red-man-s-revenge-a-tale-of-th:
R. M. Ballantyne sets The Red Man's Revenge on the Red River, in a tale tied to a great flood. Ballantyne served as a clerk of the Hudson's Bay Company at the Red River Settlement from 1841. He worked there until 1847 and came home to Edinburgh in 1848.

His letters home, full of backwoods life, pushed his family to urge a book. The Young Fur Traders, Ungava, and The Coral Island grew from that start. In his last years his pen slowed, though his quality never failed. This tale returns to the ground he knew best, the northern Canadian settlement of his youth.
22012-the-rover-boys-on-a-hunt-or-the-my:
Arthur M. Winfield, the pen name of Edward Stratemeyer, wrote The Rover Boys on a Hunt for the long Rover Boys series. It appeared in 1920. Jack Rover and his cousins are finishing the term at Putnam Hall when the story opens with a bobsled race. Christmas at home and a railroad rescue follow before the boys head north to Cedar Lodge.

Winter camp gives them hunting, ice fishing, and unwelcome visitors. Wolves prowl the woods, and a strange house deep in the trees raises questions no one can answer at first. The boys meet each scrape with jokes and teamwork. It is a brisk sample of the series fiction American boys devoured a century ago.
23223-good-blood: Ernst von Wildenbruch's Good Blood opens in a pleasant town known for its retired gentlemen. One of them, an old retired colonel, is known to everyone in town. He belongs to a colony of the superannuated, men who have settled down in this agreeable place to drag out the end of their days, wearily, in retirement.
23545-songs-of-childhood:
Walter Ramal, better known as Walter de la Mare, wrote these songs of childhood. They were first printed in nineteen hundred two by Longmans, Green, and here in a Garland facsimile from a Yale copy. Forty seven poems on subjects and experiences familiar to children fill the book, with a preface by Anthony Hecht.

De la Mare follows the Romantic dream that a child is both the most innocent and the wisest of us all, a theme Wordsworth hailed in his mighty prophet lines. The poems speak of play, fear, wonder, and small daily sights in a voice both simple and strange. Young readers and grown lovers of verse alike will enjoy the songs, which treat childhood not as a lesser age but as a clear, bright way of seeing.
23564-rookwood:
William Harrison Ainsworth wrote this novel of Rookwood, praised by Thackeray as immortal and by the New York Herald for vivid pictures of times and places. A memoir to his mother opens the book, followed by the wedding ring, a vault, a skeleton hand, the park, the hall, and Sir Reginald and Sir Piers Rookwood.

Ranulph Rookwood, Lady Rookwood, a chamber of death, and feuding brothers drive the plot, with Dick Turpin clearing Hornsey toll gate in a famed plate. Ainsworth mixes gothic horror, highwayman dash, and family curse in a tale that made his name. Readers who love old melodrama will enjoy Rookwood's vaults, secrets, and gallops, told with a gusto that still carries a reader along.
2450-boyhood:
Leo Tolstoy's Boyhood, the second part of his autobiographical trilogy, follows the young narrator from childhood into adolescence, with its confusions, friendships, and moral awakenings. The book traces school, family, and first love with the psychological honesty that would fill Tolstoy's great novels. Its episodes are small, but their feeling is large.

The trilogy's middle volume shows Tolstoy learning his art: memory rendered as moral inquiry. Readers approaching his work will find a short, accessible start. It pairs with Childhood and Youth. Tolstoy wrote the trilogy between his army service and his great novels.
2670-love-songs-of-childhood:
Eugene Field wrote these love songs of childhood for his aunt, Mrs. Belle Angler, recalling how she rocked him to sleep singing petty songs. Field tells her she was beautiful then, and more beautiful now, after years of maternity's joys and sorrows.

The poems that follow sing of babies, play, bedtime, and small wonders, in Field's tender, musical voice. They made him a favorite of American nurseries, and many were set to memory by generations of children. The book endures as a gentle classic of verse for the very young.
402-penrod:
Booth Tarkington follows twelve-year-old Penrod Schofield through a year of school, shows, and scrapes in this comic novel. Penrod, who guards his feelings behind a blank face, hates the pageant his mother forces him to join. His dog Duke, his friends, and the town's grown-ups keep pulling him into fresh trouble.

Chapters track a costume, a smallpox scare, a birthday party, and a feud with a show-off rival. Tarkington writes boyhood with fond humor, catching how a child thinks and hides thought. The book endures as a warm, funny portrait of growing up in a small American town.
4364-the-lances-of-lynwood:
Charlotte M. Yonge wrote this historical tale for young readers, drawing on Froissart's chronicle and the old French life of Bertrand du Guesclin. Her preface hopes the sketch may lead young readers to Froissart himself, not put off by how large his books are. Orthon's tale, she notes, follows Froissart almost word for word, and it resembles German and Irish legends.

The Lances of Lynwood follows a young English knight in the chivalric world of the fourteenth century, with its battles, courts, and codes. Yonge tells the tale with her usual moral care, making history into adventure. It remains a good introduction to the age of chivalry for younger readers, and for adults who enjoy it too.
5080-magnum-bonum-or-mother-carey-s-broo:
Charlotte M. Yonge's Magnum Bonum, or Mother Carey's Brood, opens with Joe Brownlow's fancy and a plea for a little teacher at Miss Heath's school. The girl has had measles last and worst, came from an asylum for officers' daughters, and has no home at all, while the house must be purified and its people go away.

She cannot travel with them, since their sister has children, and would otherwise roam from room to room before the whitewashers, in a critical state of chest. Mother Carey takes her in, and the brood's story follows. Readers get a domestic novel of kindness and family life, where a holiday guest becomes part of the household's heart.
564-the-mystery-of-edwin-drood:
Charles Dickens left his last novel unfinished at his death, and the mystery of Edwin Drood has puzzled readers ever since. Young Drood vanishes from Cloisterham, a cathedral town of deans, nuns, and opium dreams. Dickens died in 1870 with only half the novel written, leaving six monthly parts done.

Chapters follow John Jasper, Rosa Bud, and Neville Landless through suspicion, a night with Durdles, and a flight, but no ending survives. The book fascinates as much for what Dickens never wrote as for the rich, dark story he did. Readers have offered endings ever since, from stage plays to new novels that finish the tale.
5773-annals-of-a-quiet-neighbourhood:
George MacDonald narrates Annals of a Quiet Neighbourhood through a clergyman newly arrived at Marshmallows. Chapters follow despondency and consolation, a first Sunday and Monday, a coffin, visitors from the hall, Oldcastle Hall, the bishop's basin, and what the narrator preached. An organist, a Christmas party, a sermon on God and Mammon, and pupils like young Weir fill the parish year.

This gives a gentle chronicle of village life, where sermons, visits, and small kindnesses matter more than great events. MacDonald's moral imagination softens doctrine into story, letting parishioners teach the parson as much as he teaches them. The book suits readers who enjoy Victorian clerical fiction, quiet humor, and a portrait of community built one Sunday at a time.
5986-clara-hopgood:
Mark Rutherford sets his tale ten miles northeast of Eastthorpe, in Fenmarket, a town wholly in the Fens. Its roads run level, monotonous, and straight, flanked by deep stagnant ditches, and its river moves broader and slower toward the sea. The flat country shapes the story's mood.

Clara and Madge Hopgood, two young women playing chess in their mother's back parlor on a dark November afternoon in 1844, anchor the opening. Rutherford writes plainly about provincial life, family duty, and conscience. The novel follows sisters whose quiet choices carry real moral weight.
6469-queen-victoria-her-girlhood-and-wom:
Grace Greenwood writes Queen Victoria's girlhood and womanhood, dedicating the life to Camilla Toulmin, Mrs. Newton Crosland, in memory of a dear old time when the world seemed brighter. Greenwood insists Victoria's life cannot be told without a prefacing sketch of her cousin, Princess Charlotte, who would have been queen had she lived. Charlotte, lovely miracle flower of a loveless marriage, bloomed into noble womanhood amid a corrupt court's petty strifes.

Her happy girlhood, marriage to Prince Leopold, beautiful life at Claremont, and sad death prepared the way, Greenwood argues, for the fair young kinswoman who reigned twenty one years later. A mid passage admires a Sully portrait: no rigidity, no irksome state, only springy, exultant vitality and the dewy morning of life. The princeliness of youth outshines the crown she wears.
7011-the-flood:
Emile Zola's Flood speaks through Louis Roubien, seventy years old, born at Saint Jory some miles up the Garonne from Toulouse. For fourteen years he battled the earth for daily bread, until prosperity smiled and he stood last month the richest farmer in the parish. His house seemed blessed, happiness reigned, the sun was a brother, and no bad crop could be recalled.

Almost a dozen lived on the farm: Louis himself still hale, his brother Pierre the retired sergeant and old bachelor, and his sister Agathe, commanding, enormous, and gay. His son Jacques, wife Rosie, and their three daughters Aimee, Veronique, and Marie complete the household, with Aimee married to big jolly Cyprica Bouisson. The flood that gives the tale its name will break this peace.
7051-the-good-news-of-god:
Charles Kingsley preaches the good news of God in this 1887 Macmillan collection, transferred from Longman and reprinted many times since 1863. The contents open with the beatific vision, the glory of the cross, and the life of God, then the song of the three children and the eternal goodness. Worship, God's inheritance, De Profundis, and the love of God as its own reward follow.

Later sermons treat the race of life, self respect and self righteousness, true repentance, and the letter and the spirit. Heroes and heroines, the measure of the cross, the pure in heart, music, and the Christ child lead toward Christ's boyhood and the locust swarms. Kingsley preaches a warm, earnest gospel for ordinary hearers.
7280-my-boyhood:
John Burroughs wrote these sketches of boyhood and early farm life at first in self-defense, because his son Julian had set out to write them and was treading on sacred ground. Burroughs told his son he would be homesick, knowing just how he felt when he left home forty-three years before. He had stayed more or less homesick ever since, with love of old hills and of father and mother deep in his being.

Julian adds a conclusion to his father's sketches, framing a book of farm chores, seasons, and family feeling. Burroughs writes with a naturalist's eye and a son's tenderness, letting small memories carry large affection. The book reads as a return to a lost home, kept alive in prose.
7311-the-leatherwood-god:
William Dean Howells's Leatherwood God draws its historical outline largely from Judge Taneyhill's narrative in the Ohio Valley Series. Its details are often invented, and its characters are invented in their inner growth, though some rest on real persons easy to spot in that narrative. The drama follows the actual events in their main development, as a self-styled god rises among Ohio settlers.

Howells lets the tale test faith, credulity, and frontier hunger for wonder, with an illustration of the towering prophet, hair tossed like a mane, facing his flock. The novel's interest lies less in marvels than in how ordinary people answer them. It stands as a sober American study of false prophecy.
7931-all-wool-morrison-time-today-place-:
Holman Day's All-Wool Morrison, set today in the United States across twenty-four hours, is dedicated to Percival P Baxter, champion of the people's white coal. Contents run from how the Morrison broke St Ronan's rule and the threat of night through contracts, alarms, and men waiting to be shown.

Later chapters bring a mayor's word, a thin crust over boiling lava, and a rod in pickle. A square break, flarebacks of love and mob, and rifles ruling in the people's house follow, with a capitol first in shadow, then alight. Through one tense day, Day stages politics, power, and a town's fight.
832-robin-hood:
J. Walker McSpadden retold the Robin Hood legends for young readers in this clear, brisk volume. Robin becomes an outlaw, meets Little John, turns butcher to fool the Sheriff, and gathers his band in Sherwood Forest. Each chapter takes a famous exploit, from archery contests to rescues on the road.

McSpadden keeps the old ballad spirit: Robin robs the rich, aids the poor, and defies the Sheriff of Nottingham with wit and bow. The prose is plain and lively, suited to children meeting the legend first. The book remains a friendly doorway into the greenwood tales that have charmed readers for centuries.
8406-the-subterranean-brotherhood:
Julian Hawthorne opens this novel with a prisoner's footfall: a step pacing four paces in the cell above, night after night, in a sleeping jail. The narrator never sees the man or hears him speak, yet the sound becomes a bond, a brotherhood of the imprisoned. From that stark opening, the novel builds a story of confinement, guilt, and human connection behind bars.

Hawthorne, son of Nathaniel, wrote often of sin and secrecy, and here he turns to prison life itself. The book's power lies less in plot than in atmosphere: barred doors, iron walls, and the imagination filling what it cannot see. Readers of prison literature will find an early, haunting American example.
9171-slavery-ordained-of-god:
Reverend Frederick A. Ross wrote this pro-slavery book, in speeches and letters as first published, before the Civil War. His text is Romans: the powers that be are ordained of God. Ross argues in one harmonious demonstration that slavery belongs to God's government for fallen mankind, for the good of slave, master, and nation alike.

He addresses men North and South who honor the Bible and love their country, urging harmony and union on his terms. Modern readers will reject his case outright. The book remains vital evidence of how scripture was used to defend slavery, and why that defense failed.
9301-ranald-bannerman-s-boyhood:
George MacDonald wrote this boyhood tale in 1871, told by Ranald Bannerman himself. Chapters follow the glimmer of twilight, his father, Kirsty, and his first steps in life. Then comes no father, a schoolmistress defeated, and new things learned at school. Sir Worm Wymble, a kelpie, and Wandering Willie stir the boy's fancy.

Later chapters bring a fall and a dream, a bees' nest, knight-errantry, and failure, with turkey plots and old John Jamieson. A winter's ride and a peat-stack close the seasons of youth. MacDonald writes with warmth and moral clarity. The book remains a beloved Scots boy's story, tender and true.
964-the-merry-adventures-of-robin-hood:
Howard Pyle wrote these merry adventures of Robin Hood for readers who plod amid serious things. Such readers feel it shame to give themselves up, even for a few moments, to mirth in the land of Fancy. Pyle answers that life has room for innocent laughter, and he gives it in Sherwood Forest.

Robin gathers Little John, Friar Tuck, and his band, robs the rich, aids the poor, and outwits the Sheriff of Nottingham with bow and wit. Pyle's prose and pictures made this the classic Robin Hood for children. The book remains a joyful doorway into the greenwood, for readers of every age.
annals-of-a-quiet-neighbourhood:
Annals of a Quiet Neighbourhood, by George MacDonald, records a country vicar's first years among his parishioners at Marshmallows. MacDonald gives the narrator thirty four chapters of small events: despondency and consolation, a first Sunday, a first Monday, and a coffin. Visitors come from the Hall, the bishop's basin causes talk, and the new man preaches on God and Mammon to a congregation still deciding what he is.

Later chapters follow the organist, a Christmas party, and the Weir family, whose troubles fill three headings about devils in father, daughter, and vicar alike. Dr Duncan tells his story, the church rate stirs a fight, and an invalid tests everyone's patience. MacDonald writes sermons into daily life rather than the other way round: doctrine is what happens when a pastor must bury, marry, forgive, and be forgiven in one small place.
boswell-s-life-of-johnson-abridged-and-e:
James Boswell's Life of Johnson appears here abridged and edited by Charles Grosvenor Osgood, professor of English at Princeton. Osgood's preface explains his cuts: most criticism, notes, legal opinions, and letters go, while the conversation and the passages readers find by opening at random stay. Enough remains, he hopes, to illustrate the whole book.

What survives is Johnson talking: on arts propagated by Roman conquest, on biography, poetry, and men, with Boswell prompting and recording. A visitor cutting bristles from Johnson's hearth-broom as a relic shows the Doctor's fame from inside. The abridgement made the greatest English biography portable for students, and its Johnson, diverted by his own fancy, loses little of his force.
boyhood:
Leo Tolstoy continued Nikolenka's story in Boyhood, the second part of his early trilogy, in C. J. Hogarth's translation. The family leaves the estate at Petrovskoe for Moscow after the mother's death, and Nikolenka travels with his brother Woloda, their sisters, and the faithful tutor Karl Ivanitch. A thunderstorm on the road opens the boy's inner weather.

In Moscow come a grandmother's grief, bad marks at school, stolen keys, first loves, and long arguments about life. Karl Ivanitch tells his own history across three chapters. Tolstoy watches an adolescent discover vanity, cruelty, and conscience in himself, often within one page. Boyhood has less plot than Childhood and more mind: it is a diary of becoming, kept with merciless honesty.
captain-blood: Captain Blood, Rafael Sabatini's famous pirate adventure. The doctor turned buccaneer sails the Caribbean. This book preserves that swashbuckling classic. Scholars prize such firsthand sources. The paper lived through the years. Later readers can locate it.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-adam-blackwoo:
Adam Blackwood was an author born at Dunfermline, Scotland, in 1539, who died in 1613. A great-nephew of Orkney's Bishop Robert Reid, he was educated at Paris after both parents died. The bishop provided for his schooling, and Queen Mary's generosity let him finish his studies at Paris and Toulouse. At Paris he taught philosophy and published a funeral poem on Charles IX in 1574.

He also published a work on religion and government in 1575; Archbishop James Beaton then recommended him to Mary for the judgeship of the Parliament of Poitiers, where he married Catherine Courtinier. Blackwood built a good library and wrote several books, including an Apology for Kings denouncing Buchanan's views and a vigorous defence of Queen Mary, published at Paris after her death.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-adulteration-:
Adulteration of food, from Latin adulterare, to pollute, is defined as adding any non-condimental substance to a food, where that substance forms no portion of the food. Even this careful definition is imperfect, since heavily salted provisions may need soaking to remove salt, yet that is not adulteration. Food adulteration has long been practised, mentioned for bread by Pliny, who also notes Rome's trouble procuring pure wines.

Athens kept a public inspector of wines, and England and France early passed laws against bread adulteration. As far back as Edward the Confessor, public punishment awaited brewers of bad ale; adulteration's legal status rests largely on statute and varies by government. Food counts as adulterated if a substance depreciates or harms it. It also counts if cheaper matter is substituted, if a valuable constituent is removed, if it is an imitation, or if colouring improves its looks.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-anthony-of-th:
A Spanish Carmelite called A. de Olivera, Anthony of the Mother of God was born at Leon in Old-Castile and died in 1641. At the University of Alcalá de Henares, Complutum, he taught Aristotle's dialectics and natural philosophy. Together with colleagues, he set out to make an encyclopaedia for students in arts and philosophy.

That work, first styled Collegium Complutense philosophicum and printed at Alcalá in 1624, saw further editions at Frankfurt in 1629 and at Lyons in 1637, 1651, and 1668. Thomists held it in high esteem. At first it was a treatise on logic. Over time, metaphysics and moral philosophy joined it, and it served as an introduction to the Salmanticenses' great Course of Theology. Anthony is also credited with the first three volumes of that Course.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-archconfrater:
Confraternities devoted to the Precious Blood, the blood of Christ, first appeared in Spain. The life of Francis of the Infant Jesus, a Carmelite lay brother who died in 1601, mentions such a confraternity at Valencia. A few years on they must have been numerous, since Anna of St. Augustine, who died in 1624, welcomed collectors of alms for Precious Blood confraternities erected in many places. Ravenna in Italy had one very early, and Rome had one under Gregory XIII, later merged with the Gonfalone.

The archconfraternity as it now stands owes its origin to Mgr. Albertini, then serving at San Nicola in Carcere, Rome, where devotions to the Precious Blood had been held since 1708. Moved by the temporal and spiritual misery of the French Revolution, he joined on 8 December 1808 all willing to meditate frequently on the Precious Blood into a society. That society grew into an archconfraternity able to affiliate others.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-association-o:
The Association of the Holy Childhood is a children's association for foreign missions, founded twenty years after the Society for the Propagation of the Faith, in 1843. It was founded by Charles de Forbin-Janson, bishop of Nancy in France, as the Society of the Holy Childhood. Its end is twofold. First, to gather little Christian children around the Infant Jesus from tender years. Growing in age and strength and imitating Jesus their master, they practise charity toward their own perfection.

Second, by charity and enduring liberality, those same children may help save from death and sin the many thousand children in pagan countries such as China. Those children are neglected by parents and cast away to die without baptism. The association seeks baptism for abandoned ones and, should they live, training as craftsmen, teachers, doctors, or other members of Christian communities. The entry presents child charity organized for child rescue.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bl-thomas-she:
Blessed Thomas Sherwood, a martyr, is the subject of this 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia entry. Born in London in 1551, he died at Tyburn on 7 February 1578. His parents also suffered for conscience, both enduring prison for the faith. After school in 1566 he helped his father, a woollen draper, for ten years, then set out for Douai to study for the priesthood.

Spotted in Chancery Lane, he was betrayed by George Marten and examined on the pope's bull and twice racked to learn where he had heard Mass. Cast naked into a dark, foul dungeon on bare earth, with only straw from a friend's pleading, he kept a cheerful courage. Tried on 3 February for denying the queen's supremacy, he was executed four days later.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-brothers-hosp:
The Brothers Hospitallers of Saint John of God carry on their founder's hospital charity from Granada across the world. John, born at Montemor Novo in 1495, turned to God's service at forty, founded his first hospital at Granada, and served the sick with heroic charity until his death in 1550. Canonized in 1690, he became patron of the dying and of all hospitals in 1898.

Antoni Martin succeeded him, Philip II funded hospitals at Madrid, Cordova, and beyond, and Pius V approved the order under Augustine's rule in 1572. Gregory XIII gave them Rome's Hospital of Saint John Calybita in 1584 as mother-house, and Marie de' Medici founded their first French hospital at Paris in 1601. The Revolution expelled them from forty hospitals holding 4,125 patients, yet the order now counts eleven provinces, 102 hospitals, and 12,978 beds.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-charles-franc:
Charles-Francois Gounod, born at Paris in 1818 and dead there in 1893, stands among the great French composers of the nineteenth century. His father died while Charles was still a child, leaving his education to his mother. At the Lycée Saint-Louis he ranked among the best scholars. His musical gifts were carefully developed by his mother.

At thirteen his mother took him to Rossini's Otello, and that same year Mozart's Don Juan raised him to high enthusiasm. Mozart remained his ideal throughout his career, and Beethoven's Pastoral and Ninth Symphonies also left lasting marks. After study at the Conservatoire under Reicha and Lesueur, he returned to Paris in 1842. His career then turned to the operatic stage, where his lyrical, sentimental treatment of Faust, Romeo and Juliet, and Polyeucte became the widest expression of French Romanticism.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-christopher-h:
An entry on Christopher Holywood, Jesuit, born at Artane near Dublin in 1559. His family took its name from Holywood village. Holywood studied at Padua, then joined the Society of Jesus in 1579 at Dôle, to teach Scripture and theology at Pont-à-Mousson, Ferrara, and Padua, where he knew Bellarmine. Sent to Ireland in 1598, he was seized on the way and held in the Gatehouse, the Tower, and Wisbech Castle.

Freed after Elizabeth's death, Holywood reached Ireland on Saint Patrick's Eve 1604 and published two Latin controversial works at Antwerp that year. As superior of his brethren, in an Ireland without bishops, he reconciled the lapsed, settled quarrels, and healed wounds left by persecution. Only four Jesuits stood in Ireland when he landed, but forty-two worked there at his death in 1626, with sixty more in training or teaching abroad. His letters light up the country's history.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-congregation-:
Ulrich Müller's entry follows the Most Precious Blood congregation, secular priests in community whose principal aim is missions and retreats. Members take no vows, held by charity's bond and a promise not to leave without permission. Pius VII, returning from exile, distressed at Rome's state, desired missions throughout the Papal States. He chose Gaspare del Bufalo with zealous priests in 1814, assigning San Felice convent at Giano, founded 15 August 1815.

New houses opened, and in 1820 six missions rose in the Campagna for banditti. Leo XII's 1823 election checked growth, misinformation clouding the society's standing. America received it in 1844 at Cincinnati Bishop Purcell's request, with year-long probation before brothers take fidelity promises or students begin study. Statistics count Italy's three provinces and fifteen houses, Rome, Albano, San Paolo leading, plus Spain's one province. A separate Mantua knight-order of 1608, founded by Duke Vincenzo Gonzaga with Paul V's approval, closes it.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-congregations:
The entry surveys Precious Blood congregations, opening with the Bernadines, nuns no longer in existence, founded by Mother Ballou with Saint Francis de Sales from reformed Cistercianesses. Spiehermans founded the Daughters at Sittard, Holland, in 1862, approved by Leo XIII's decree of 12 July 1890. Girls' education and sick care form their main object. A red girdle and a cross marked F.P.S. on red ribbon distinguish them. Cardinal Mazzella served as protector, Koningbosch holds the mother-house, and they assist Holy Ghost Fathers in German East Africa, with no American foundation yet.

Sister Adorers, established on 14 September 1861, lead a further section. Sisters of the Precious Blood at Gurtweil in Baden and Grisons, Switzerland, date to 1833 under Maria Anna Brunner with her son. Statistics for 1911 count 592 professed sisters, 48 novices, 26 postulants, and 6,954 pupils across Cleveland, Fort Wayne, Kansas City, Nashville, Saint Joseph, and Tucson dioceses.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-dominic-of-th:
Dominic of the Mother of God, born Domenico Barberi near Viterbo in 1792, was a Passionist theologian. His peasant parents died while he was small, and his uncle adopted him, youngest of six children. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry tells how he herded sheep and worked the farm, learning letters from a kind Capuchin and a country lad of his age. He had no regular schooling until he joined the Passionists.

Deeply religious from childhood, he felt called to the institute and to England, where he labored for the conversion of the country. He died near Reading in 1849. His letters on the English mission were printed as a supplement to the Oratorian life of Saint Paul of the Cross. The entry points readers to lives of this apostle of England.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ephod:
The ephod was a garment named in Scripture, differing with its use by the high priest, by others at worship, or in idolatrous cult. For the high priest, joining Bible evidence with Josephus and Egyptian monuments, the entry distinguishes three parts: a waistcoat or bodice, two shoulder pieces, and a girdle. The bodice was a cloth bound round the body to the waist.

Its stuff was fine-twisted linen, embroidered with violet, purple, and scarlet twice-dyed threads, woven through with gold. The ephod must not be mixed up with the tunic of the ephod, a violet frock worn beneath it. Its skirt was edged with pomegranates and bells that sounded as the priest ministered. Nor is it the breastplate, a span square, set with four rows of stones naming the twelve tribes. It held the Urim and Thummim, by which the priest sought the Lord's counsel.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-etymology-of-:
God can be defined as the proper name of the one Supreme and Infinite Personal Being, Creator and Ruler of the universe, to whom man owes worship. It is also the common name of beings in polytheistic religions to whom Divine attributes and worship are ascribed. It is also the name applied to an idol as the image or dwelling-place of a god.

The root-meaning, from Gothic gheu and Sanskrit hub or emu, to invoke or sacrifice to, is either the one invoked or the one sacrificed to. From roots div, to shine, and thes, to implore, come deva, dyaus, deus, theos, and dia, all generic names. Also from such roots come Zeus, Jupiter, Tiu or Tiw, surviving in Tuesday, Janus, Diana, and pagan deities' names. The common Semitic name, el in Hebrew, ilu in Babylonian, and ilah in Arabic, probably means the strong or mighty one.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-existence-of-:
Existence of God is a long article in two great parts: God as known by natural reason, and God as known by faith. It first states the problem against formal atheism, which it calls self-refuting, and against virtual atheism. That covers Spencer's agnosticism, which admits an Absolute but calls it unknowable, and pantheism in materialist, idealist, and mixed forms.

Among theists it weighs whether God is proved by plain inference from effect to cause, or by intuition and moral feeling. Kant denied the classic proofs to pure reason but postulated God for practical reason, a move the article says hurt theism. It then sets out proofs from causality, design, conscience, and universal consent, plus the ontological proof. The second part turns to Scripture, church councils, and whether God can be known at all.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-feast-of-the-:
The Most Precious Blood feast honours the Blood of Christ on July's first Sunday. At first only the Fathers of the Precious Blood kept its Office alone. Later it joined the Fridays of Lent in many dioceses and parishes. Baltimore's fourth provincial council adopted it in 1840.

Pius IX, exiled at Gaeta in 1849, heard Don Giovanni Merlini's plea for the feast. Rather than vow, the pope extended it at once to all Christendom. The decree of 10 August 1849 fixed it to July's first Sunday. That Sunday had fallen on 30 June, the day French troops retook Rome.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-friends-of-go:
The Friends of God were circles of devout men and women in the fourteenth-century Rhineland who sought holiness together. Born at Basle between 1339 and 1343, the movement spread down the Rhine to Strasburg, Cologne, and the Netherlands. Priests and layfolk alike joined, bound by nothing but a shared hunger for the inner life and the conversion of sinners.

From these circles rose the great school of German mystics, led by the preacher John Tauler and the writer Henry Suso. Their sermons, letters, and treatises count among the finest German prose of the age, rooted in the teaching of Saint Thomas. But a lay member, Rulman Merswin, later spread doubtful tales of a hidden master, and the whole group fell into disrepute.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-gaspard-mermi:
Gaspard Mermillod, bishop of Lausanne and cardinal, fought Geneva's Radical government for the Church's freedom. Born at Carouge in 1824, he was schooled by Jesuits at Fribourg. He became a Geneva curate in 1847, founded two Catholic journals, and built Notre-Dame, still Geneva's chief church, between 1851 and 1859 with gifts from all Christendom.

Made auxiliary bishop in 1864, Mermillod served Geneva freely for seven years and founded Oblate sisters for poor working girls. When Rome made him independent administrator, the canton banned his acts, deposed him even as parish priest, and finally expelled him to Ferney in France. He returned only after his rival's death, and full relations resumed when he became cardinal in 1890.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-god:
God is a doctrinal article on the name, existence, nature, and relation to the universe of God, with the Blessed Trinity as its crown. It opens with the root-meaning of the word, derived from Gothic and Sanskrit roots. A Catholic Encyclopedia article argues that dogmatic atheism refutes itself and has never won reasoned assent from any considerable number of men.

By deductive analysis it treats the infinity, unity, and simplicity of God, with remarks on divine personality. It holds the world essentially dependent on God as Creator of its whole substance. It holds its continuance at every moment due to his sustaining power. The Trinity is presented as the central doctrine of Christianity: in the unity of the Godhead, three truly distinct Persons, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-good:
Good is one of those primary ideas which cannot be strictly defined, used first as an adjective and second as a substantive. French marks the distinction with bon and le bien, and English keeps it by prefixing an article to the substantive use. A Catholic Encyclopedia article begins from everyday uses and presses toward the metaphysical question of the good.

We call a tool good if it serves its purpose, an efficient means to a desired result. We call a thing good if it fully possesses the perfections proper to its nature. A result desired for itself is a good, an end of action. The chain of means and ends must end in objects desired for themselves. Finally we speak of good conduct, a good man, and a good intention, where the adjective carries a moral sense no utilitarian reduction captures.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-hakon-the-goo:
Norway's King Hakon the Good, youngest son of Harold Fairhair, ruled from about 935 to 960 after a childhood at the court of Athelstan of England. They gave him his nickname Adelstenfostre and a fine education. When his harsh half-brother Eric Bloodaxe fled before discontented nobles, Hakon won the throne by promising the jarls their old rights and the freemen clemency.

Reforms in justice, government, the army, trade, and deep-sea fishing followed, with Jämtland and Värmland annexed. His Christian mission faltered: raised a Christian, he pressed the new faith until pagan strength forced him to tolerate sacrifices and even join them. Wounded by an arrow at Fitje while repelling Eric's sons, he died commending his enemy Harold as successor and was buried as a warrior in a mound.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-herod:
Herod was the name of a family of rulers who loom large in the New Testament and in Jewish history, and this entry surveys them one by one. Herod the Great, son of the Idumaean Antipater, won the crown of Judea from the Roman senate in 40 BC through the favour of Octavian and Antony. He held power by shifting with Rome's changing masters, built on a grand scale, and ordered cruelties that darkened his final years.

Later Herods include Antipas, tetrarch of Galilee, who had John the Baptist killed after the prophet rebuked his marriage to Herodias. Agrippa I persecuted the early church, and Agrippa II heard St. Paul's defence. The entry draws on Josephus throughout, weighs conflicting accounts, and shows how one family's fortunes tracked the rise of Roman power in Judea.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-holy-synod:
The Holy Synod, in full the Most Holy Directing Synod, is the council governing the Church of Russia and, by its example, many other Orthodox churches. Summoning a synod to settle grave questions goes back to the apostles meeting at Jerusalem over Gentile converts. Bishops, metropolitans, and patriarchs all called synods as need arose, and general councils represented the whole Catholic world from 325 onward.

Yet those synods met only briefly, for one or a few burning questions. The predecessors of modern Holy Synods lie rather in permanent councils at the courts of chief bishops, which formed naturally without harming the bishop's monarchical rule. The entry traces how that permanent council model grew into the governing synod of the Russian church and its Orthodox imitators.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-hood:
A hood means a soft, cone-shaped, brimless covering for the whole head apart from the face. It may stand alone as a garment or form part of a cloak. Worn on its own, it commonly flares below into a cape of sorts, open at the front at times and at other times shut save for the face hole. Romans called it cucullus, a Celtic word, worn above all by drivers, herdsmen, and labourers.

All classes wore it as part of Roman cloaks. In the Middle Ages it was common in France, Germany, and England among clerics and layfolk, men and women, high and low. Monks and mendicant friars wore it daily, as part of their religious dress. In the thirteenth and fourteenth centuries it often ended in a long peak, the liripipe. Hats later displaced it, but old orders kept it, and Capuchins take their name from their hood.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jasper-and-jo:
Jasper Heywood, poet and translator, was born in London in 1535 and died at Naples in 1598. As a boy he served as page of honor to Princess Elizabeth, later queen. Sent to Oxford in 1547, he took a bachelor's degree in 1553 and a master's in 1558. In 1554 he was chosen probationary fellow of Merton College, where he shone in disputations, in verse renderings of Seneca's dramas, and as Lord of Misrule at Christmas.

Anthony à Wood reports that he and his brother were wild for a spell. Jasper gave up his fellowship to head off expulsion in 1558, and later that year was chosen fellow of All Souls. Soon he gave that up over refusal to comply with Elizabeth's new religious order. He stands paired here with his father John, dramatist to his poet-translator, across Elizabethan religious change. After ordination as a priest, he was received into the Society of Jesus at Rome in 1562.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-kingdom-of-go:
The Kingdom of God, called the Kingdom of Heaven in Matthew, sums up the Old Testament's deepest teaching. Kingdom here means rule or sway as much as territory: God himself reigns, and earthly kings rule only under him.

The idea runs from the theocracy sketched in Exodus, through Samuel's warning that Israel rejected God as king, and Nathan's promise to David's line. In the Psalms, God's throne stands in heaven. Prophets stress the same kingship, and Daniel's vision of one like a son of man receiving rule over all evil powers shaped what Christ's hearers expected. A rival hope, a temporal Messiah crushing nations, grew beside it, while the Book of Wisdom shows the rule lived as a just life.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-mazenod:
Charles Joseph Eugene de Mazenod, Bishop of Marseilles and founder of the Oblates of Mary Immaculate, was born at Aix in Provence in 1782 and died at Marseilles in 1861. Sprung from a noble southern family, he showed early piety and a high, independent spirit. The Revolution drove him into exile in Italy for some years. He then studied for the priesthood, though he was his family's last representative.

Ordained at Amiens in 1811, he grieved at religion's ruin among the masses after the Revolution. In 1816 he gathered a small band to preach in the local tongue and teach the rural folk of Provence. Leo XII approved the band in 1826 as the Congregation of the Oblates of Mary Immaculate. After aiding his aged uncle, the Bishop of Marseilles, Mazenod was consecrated titular bishop in 1832 and later held the Marseilles see himself.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-nature-and-at:
The Nature and Attributes of God treats first what natural reason knows: infinity, unity, simplicity and divine personality. Then it treats what faith adds: eternity, immensity and omnipresence, immutability, divine knowledge, divine will, and intellect and will in providence, predestination and reprobation. Reason begins from a self-existent personal First Cause distinct from matter and mind.

To say God is infinite means he is unlimited in every perfection, with every perfection his in the highest way. That differs from infinite time or space, meaning duration or extension with no fixed limit. The entry works through each attribute with careful thought, guarding against confusions, and showing how the God of the philosophers and the God of faith cohere in one Being.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-nemrod:
Nemrod, also Nimrod, is the descendant of Cush, son of Ham, shown in Genesis 10 as founder of the Babylonian empire and a mighty hunter before the Lord. Hunter may be taken strictly, since Babylonian princes hunted wild beasts, or as warrior, since the original word gibbor means hero. His name has not yet been found in cuneiform inscriptions.

Attempts to identify him with known figures rest on more or less plausible conjectures. Some scholars, Delitzsch, Hommel and Haupt among them, identify him with Gilgamesh, hero of the Babylonian epic, often shown strangling a lion. Gilgamesh subdues the ox-faced Eabani, makes him his companion, triumphs over the tyrant Humbaba, and slays a monster sent by Anu and Ishtar. Like Nemrod he reigns over Erech, but the texts omit Babylon, Accad and Calneh from Genesis 10.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-poor-servants:
The Poor Servants of the Mother of God are a religious congregation founded in 1808 by Mother Mary Magdalen Taylor with Lady Georgiana Fullerton. Taylor was the daughter of a Church of England clergyman. As one of Florence Nightingale's nurses in the Crimea she met the Catholic faith among the soldiers, and on returning to England she entered the Church.

Her friendship with Lady Georgiana led to a congregation for work among London's poor, then served by a single convent. Cardinal Manning approved and encouraged it, the Jesuits guided its spiritual training, and Leo XIII approved it in 1885. Its sisters visit the poor, teach in parochial schools, nurse the sick, and run refuges for women, with houses from London and Dublin to Rome and Florence.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-precious-bloo:
The Precious Blood is our Divine Saviour's blood. At the Last Supper Jesus gives it the same life giving power as His flesh. Peter, John, and above all Paul treat it as one with Jesus' Passion and Death. It thus forms part of the Sacred Humanity, joined in person to the Trinity's Second Person.

In the fifteenth century divines asked whether the blood shed in the Passion stayed joined to the Word. If a core part of the Sacred Humanity, it could never part from the Word; if a mere attendant, it could. Dominicans held the first view, Franciscans the second. But since Trent called the body and blood of Jesus parts of Christ the Lord, thought has run with the Dominicans. Faber writes that the blood itself, as blood, was more than a mere attendant of the flesh.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-presence-of-g:
All sound devotion must rest on truths of faith. First, faith holds that God's Essence is everywhere, in all things, through His Immensity. Faith also holds Him present in the souls of the just in a special, real, substantial way. 

To put ourselves in God's presence, or to live in God's presence, means to grow actually aware of God as present, or at least to live as if thus aware. It is a plain act, holding the print of the unseen Being with whom we hold direct dealings. His goodness to us is sure, and He loves us with an everlasting love. He keeps a special providence among us, is present everywhere, and, in Cardinal Newman's words, is heart reading, heart changing, ever open to our approach.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-priesthood:
Priest, from Greek presbyteros, elder, matched against neoteros, younger, means in its hieratic sense the Latin sacerdos, the Greek iereus, and the Hebrew kahane. It marks a male person called to the Deity's direct service and licensed for public worship, above all to offer sacrifice. To call the magicians, prophets, and medicine men of primitive faiths priests misuses the word. Sacrifice is priesthood's core correlative, so mere leaders of public prayer or shrine keepers have no claim to the name.

 Oldest among pagan faiths is India's, with four divisions: Vedism, Brahminism, Buddhism, and Hinduism.  St Peter calls the faithful a holy priesthood and a kingly priesthood, but the text means a figurative priesthood only. Hence the Catholic clergy alone, the entry holds, bear the name priest in truth, since they alone offer a true and real sacrifice, the Holy Mass.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-rood:
Rood, from Anglo-Saxon Rod or Rode, meaning cross, often means the True Cross itself. More broadly, the word denotes a big crucifix flanked by figures of Our Lady and St John, set above the choir entrance in medieval churches. Roods were often very large, to be seen from all parts of the church, set on a gallery, screen, or beam spanning the chancel arch.

No certain evidence dates the rood's antiquity. A silver crucifix set up by Leo III in St Peter's at Rome in 795 is sometimes claimed as an early example. Nothing proves it counted as a medieval rood. The great rood was common in almost every Western church by the thirteenth century, and certainly by the fourteenth. Figures of Mary and John were added about the fifteenth century, recalling John 19:25. Roods were usually carved wood, painted or gilded.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-son-of-god:
Son of God is a title that runs through both Testaments with shifting shades of meaning. This substantial entry follows each of those meanings in turn. In the Old Testament the word son could mark any close bond. Angels, just men, and descendants of Seth could all be called sons of God. So could the whole people of Israel, and kings received the title as God's chosen rulers.

The entry then traces how the phrase deepens in the New Testament, where it belongs to Christ in a unique sense. It works through the scriptural passages and the theological questions the title raises. Readers who want to see why a familiar phrase carries so much weight will find its history laid out step by step, from Hebrew idiom to Christian doctrine.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-disibod:
Disibod, an Irish bishop who died in 700, carried his country's monastic ways into the Rhineland, and this short entry follows him there. Born about 619, he crossed to the continent around 653 and settled in the valley of the Nahe, near Bingen. Though he lived as a hermit, a community grew around him in beehive cells built in Irish fashion on the mountain slopes. The Catholic Encyclopedia piece of 1913 notes his life was written in 1170 by Hildegard, from her visions.

Before his death he saw a church raised and served by monks under the Rule of Columba. He was chosen abbot-bishop, and the house took his name as Mount Disibod, later Disenberg, in the diocese of Mainz. Miracles cluster around his memory, and even his death date is disputed. Some place it on 8 September, reading 8 July as the day his relics were moved in 754, with Boniface present.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-john-of-go:
John of God, founder of hospital care at Granada, lived soldier, shepherd, and would-be African ransomer before he found his work. Born at Montemor-o-Novo in Portugal on 8 March 1495 to devout parents, he followed a Spanish priest to Oropeza at nine and was left with the chief shepherd there. The Catholic Encyclopedia piece of 1913 dates his death at Granada to 8 March 1550, his fifty-fifth birthday.

To escape his master's persistent offer of his daughter's hand, John served in Charles V's army, then in a regiment bound for Austria against the Turks. Later he grieved at his birthplace for his mother's early death, shepherded at Seville, and travelled toward Gibraltar, hoping to ransom African captives with his own liberty. At Granada he built a hospital, tending patients with scrupulous care, aided by charitable priests and physicians. Heavenly guests, the entry says, sometimes lightened his herculean tasks.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-synod:
A synod, from Greek synodos, assembly, is a general term for church gatherings under hierarchical authority to discuss and decide faith, morals, or discipline. It matches Latin concilium, used by Tertullian a century before synodus appears in the so-called Apostolic canons, so the two words are synonyms. Bishops of the whole world under the pope form an ecumenical or general synod, the only body rightly called holy synod.

Provincial synods gather a province under its metropolitan, national or plenary synods gather a whole nation, and mixed councils join church and secular dignitaries. The diocesan synod differs from all: other councils give bishops a deciding vote, but there the bishop alone votes and legislates. Benedict XIV's De Synodo Dioecesana remains the classic work, and the entry deals mainly with diocesan synods.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-the-bridge-bu:
Bridge-building as an act of piety fills this curious entry, centred on religious associations of the twelfth and thirteenth centuries.
